chapters.title: Chapter 2: Ito Calculus: The Rules for Working With Randomness

lessons.title: Common Ito Calculus Mistakes and How to Spot Them

children.text: "Before we get to Black-Scholes," the interviewer says, closing round two, "let's make sure you don't make the mistakes everyone makes the first time they learn this." This lesson introduces no new theory. It rounds up the specific, recurring errors this chapter has already flagged along the way, puts them in one place, and adds one final tool, Ito's product rule, that Chapter 3's hedging argument needs and this chapter has not yet given you.

body.text: Almost every first-time mistake with Ito's lemma comes from unconsciously reverting to ordinary calculus instincts: dropping the correction term, dropping its 1/2, or setting (dW)^2 to zero. Naming each mistake explicitly, once, is usually enough to stop making it.

children.text: Five Mistakes This Chapter Already Warned You About

body.caption: A compact reference to this chapter's recurring mistakes

cells: Forgetting the Ito correction term entirely
Writing df = f'(X)dX only, exactly the ordinary chain rule, silently treating (dX)² as negligible
Writing the correction as b²f''(X)dt instead of (1/2)b²f''(X)dt, doubling it
Treating dW like an ordinary infinitesimal
Setting (dW)² = 0, or writing dW/dt as an ordinary derivative
Treating Qn → t and Var(W(t)) = t as the same statement, when one is pathwise and the other is distributional
Mixing up CAGR and arithmetic mean when calibrating μ
Feeding a compound annual growth rate into μ directly, when it actually corresponds to μ - σ²/2

children.text: A Sixth, New One: Ito's Product Rule

Chapter 3's central derivation needs one more tool this chapter hasn't given you yet: a rule for differentiating the PRODUCT of two stochastic processes, exactly what a hedged portfolio made of a stock position and an option position is. The ordinary product rule, d(XY) = X dY + Y dX, is missing precisely the kind of term this entire chapter has been warning you not to drop.

Apply the two-variable version of Ito's lemma to f(x, y) = xy. Its partial derivatives are f_x = y, f_y = x, f_xx = 0, f_yy = 0, and the cross-partial f_xy = 1. Ito's lemma for two variables carries a cross term, (∂²f/∂x∂y)·dX·dY, alongside the two familiar second-order terms, and here that cross term is the only second-order piece that survives.

body.latex: d(XY) = Y\,dX + X\,dY + \tfrac{1}{2}(0)(dX)^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0)(dY)^2 + (1)\,dX\,dY \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; d(XY) = X\,dY + Y\,dX + dX\,dY
body.caption: Ito's product rule: the ordinary product rule, plus a covariation term

children.text: The extra term, dX·dY, is computed with the exact same multiplication rules from Lesson 2, extended to two processes. If dX = a1 dt + b1 dW and dY = a2 dt + b2 dW, driven by the same Wiener process W, then dX·dY = b1 b2 (dW)² = b1 b2 dt, since every dt·dt and dt·dW cross term still vanishes. If X and Y are instead driven by two independent Wiener processes, this term drops to exactly zero, since independent Brownian motions have zero cross-variation, and the ordinary product rule turns out to be correct after all. The mistake is subtle precisely because it depends on context: whether the two processes share the same source of randomness.

body.latex: dX\,dY = \begin{cases} b_1 b_2\, dt & \text{same Wiener process } W \\ \rho\, b_1 b_2\, dt & \text{correlated } W_1, W_2,\ \text{correlation } \rho \\ 0 & \text{independent } W_1, W_2 \end{cases}
body.caption: The covariation term, depending on how X and Y share their randomness

body.text: Chapter 3's very next lesson builds a hedged portfolio out of a stock and an option written on that same stock, driven by the exact same Wiener process. That is exactly the case where dX·dY does not vanish, and skipping this product rule there would silently break the entire hedging argument before it starts.

body.title: Before You Apply Ito's Lemma
steps: Identify a(X,t) and b(X,t) directly from the SDE dX = a dt + b dW.
Compute f'(X) and f''(X), or all relevant partial derivatives if f also depends on t.
Write the full formula: df = [f_t + a·f_x + (1/2)·b²·f_xx] dt + b·f_x dW, never dropping the (1/2)·b²·f_xx term.
Never set (dW)² to zero; it stands for dt, not 0, in every Ito calculation.
If f is a product or function of two stochastic processes, check whether dX·dY vanishes (independent Wiener processes) or survives (same or correlated ones) before dropping it.

body.title: Spot the bug
body.question: A student is asked to find d(S²) for geometric Brownian motion, dS = μS dt + σS dW. They write: d(S²) = 2S dS = 2S(μS dt + σS dW) = 2μS² dt + 2σS² dW. What mistake did they make?
options: They forgot to include the drift term entirely
They applied only the ordinary chain rule, omitting the Ito correction term, (1/2)(2)(σS)² dt = σ²S² dt
They forgot the factor of 1/2, doubling the correction term
They incorrectly set (dW)² equal to dt instead of 0
body.explanation: With f(x) = x², f'(x) = 2x and f''(x) = 2. The correct application of Ito's lemma gives d(S²) = [2S(μS) + (1/2)(2)(σS)²] dt + 2S(σS) dW = (2μ + σ²)S² dt + 2σS² dW. The student's answer is missing the entire +σ²S² dt correction term, having applied the ordinary chain rule, d(S²) = 2S dS, as if S were a smooth, deterministic function.

body.title: Apply the product rule's covariation term
body.prompt: X and Y are both driven by the same Wiener process W. At a moment when X = 100 and Y = 50, dX = 0.2X dt + 0.2X dW and dY = 0.1Y dt + 0.3Y dW. What is the coefficient of dt in dX·dY at that moment? (Use dX·dY = b1·b2·dt, with b1 = 0.2X and b2 = 0.3Y.)
body.explanation: b1 = 0.2 × 100 = 20, and b2 = 0.3 × 50 = 15. Since X and Y share the same Wiener process, dX·dY = b1·b2·dt = 20 × 15 × dt = 300 dt. The coefficient of dt is 300. Forgetting this term entirely, by applying the ordinary product rule instead, would drop this 300 dt piece completely.

cards.definition: d(XY) = X dY + Y dX + dX dY, the stochastic generalization of the ordinary product rule, with an extra covariation term, dX dY, that vanishes only when X and Y are driven by independent Wiener processes.
The generalization of quadratic variation to two processes; for dX = a1 dt + b1 dW and dY = a2 dt + b2 dW sharing the same W, it equals b1 b2 dt.

cards.term: CAGR vs arithmetic mean (as a calibration trap)
cards.definition: A compound annual growth rate corresponds to a GBM's log-drift, μ - σ²/2, not to μ itself; using it directly as μ understates the model's true drift by roughly σ²/2.

points: Chapter 2, in full: SDEs generalize ODEs by adding a Wiener noise term (Lesson 1); Ito's lemma corrects the ordinary chain rule with an extra (1/2)b²f_xx dt term (Lesson 2); that correction falls directly out of a full Taylor expansion, with only Δt-order terms surviving (Lesson 3); applied to ln(S) for geometric Brownian motion, it yields the exact, lognormal closed-form solution S(t) = S(0)exp[(μ-σ²/2)t + σW(t)] (Lesson 4).

The recurring mistakes in this chapter are all variations on one theme: reverting to ordinary calculus instincts, dropping the correction term, dropping its 1/2, or setting (dW)² to zero instead of dt.
Ito's product rule, d(XY) = X dY + Y dX + dX dY, adds a covariation term that survives whenever X and Y share the same or correlated Wiener process, and vanishes only for independent ones.

This product rule is not optional background: Chapter 3's very next lesson differentiates a hedged portfolio built from a stock and an option on that same stock, exactly the case where the covariation term does not vanish.

Chapter 3 now has every tool this course set out to build: Brownian motion, Ito's lemma, and the exact GBM solution, ready to be assembled into the Black-Scholes partial differential equation and formula.
